title: What should you ask first in a revenue drop case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a revenue drop case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: When a client's sales fall, the instinct is to jump to fixes. The better move is to find out exactly where the drop is coming from first.
body:
The first question to ask

Which stream, segment or region is falling?

How to build your structure

  1. Split revenue into its streams (products, segments, regions) and find which one fell
  2. Break that stream into number of customers × spend per customer
  3. Look for the cause: the market, customers, the company itself, or competitors

The trap most people fall into

Explaining 'revenue' as one number.

An example

A cinema chain's revenue is down 12%. Do not stop at "revenue fell". Split it: tickets, food and drink, advertising. Then split tickets into visits times average price. If visits are flat but food spend per visit has dropped, you are looking at a very different problem from fewer people coming at all.

How it sounds in an interview

Revenue is made of a few streams, so I'd first find which one fell, then split it into number of customers and spend per customer.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the profitability framework.

Two prompts to try

A national bank's mortgage applications are down 20% this year. Why?

Show a model structure
  • Market: Total applications in the market: rates, house prices, transactions; Is everyone down 20%, or just us?
  • Our offer: Rates and fees vs rivals; Loan-to-value limits, product range
  • Channels: Brokers: are they placing less with us?; Online and branch: traffic, conversion
  • Process: Time to decision, approval rate (brokers avoid slow or strict lenders); Drop-off during the application

Where to start: The market first: if all banks are down 20%, it is not our problem to fix.

The trap: Jumping to marketing ideas before checking whether the whole market fell.

A pharma company's new drug is selling 40% below forecast.

Show a model structure
  • Doctors: Awareness and trust in the data; Who prescribes: specialists vs family doctors
  • Patients: How many are diagnosed and eligible; was the forecast realistic?; Price, side effects, stopping early
  • Payers: Approval for reimbursement; Restrictions: only after other drugs fail
  • Competition: Rival drugs and generics; Their pricing and contracts

Where to start: Payers: if insurers restrict it, doctors and patients can do little.

The trap: Assuming it is a marketing problem when access and reimbursement usually decide.
outro: Small things like this add up. Try it in your next practice case and notice how it changes the conversation. Practise this case type in the free casebook: every case has a worked answer.
